newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian markets shrug off Thai float news.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian markets shrug off Thai float news.

text.p: Indonesian markets on Wednesday shrugged off news of Thailand's decision to float the baht, as strong domestic fundamentals helped to stabilise initial knee-jerk declines.

Economists said Indonesia's healthy trade surplus, low inflation, comfortable foreign exchange reserves and prudent macroeconomic policies would help the country combat problems of the kind that have hit Thailand.
The rupiah weakened to 2,445 against the dollar just ahead of a news conference that Thailand held to announce it would allow the value of the baht to be set by market forces.
But it soon recovered to opening levels of around 2,433 as investors realised that the Thai move did not signal a one-off devaluation.
The Jakarta stock market was also little affected although some profit-taking pared gains after the composite index raced to its third new intra-day high in three days in early trade.
In afternoon trade, the index was down 0.43 percent at 728.48 points, off the 734.02 record.
"I don't see any direct impact of the Thai baht in the Jakarta stock market today," said Naotaka Ikeda, director of Asian Development Securities (ADS) brokerage.
Another broker, who works for a European securities firm, said the fall in the index was mainly due to technical profit-taking.
"After hitting a record high for three consecutive days, there should be some consolidation," he said.

"Indonesia is in a far stronger position (than Thailand). In a fundamental sense, the contrasts are flattering to Indonesia," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currencies at BZW Barclays in Singapore.
On Wednesday, Jakarta announced that the consumer price index had fallen 0.17 percent month-on-month in June after a 0.19 percent rise in May.
The trade surplus had increased to $590.5 million in April from $243.3 million in March.
Daragh Maher, an economist at ING Barings in Singapore, said he was quite surprised how well the rupiah held up during the day's turmoil.

"I guess you could say that over the last two to three months when other currencies in the region were under a lot of pressure by virtue of the baht, actually the pressure we saw on the rupiah has been more election-related," he said.
"With the election now out of the way, people are more comfortable with rupiah risk," he said, adding that even if there was a knockdown effect from external factors, it would be short-lived.
Indonesia held general elections on May 29 and formally announced last month that the ruling Golkar party had romped to a massive victory.
The win bolstered the country's financial markets, which saw it as a sign of continuing stability.
Trisiladi Supriyanto, vice president at the Bank of America in Jakarta, said Indonesia and Thailand were not directly comparable in terms of economic fundamentals.
"We have low inflation and a manageable current account deficit. Thailand is (only) comparable because of the location and (because it is) a close trade partner," Supriyanto said.
"If the Thai currency were attacked, there would be implications on the rupiah," he added.
Supple also said he saw some instability in regional currency markets in the short-term.

"The feeling is it would take months before we see the situation stabilise. We are going to see prolonged weakness in the baht and therefore prolonged instability in some of the regional currencies," Supple said.
"On the fundamental side, it's not justified. But an event risk has been created. The danger is some weakness could set in on account of some current account deficits in the region."
